summary: Deep technical session on long-context (128k+) runtime performance. transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour. quick intros?
[00:12] Samantha (Atlas CTO): hi all, samantha here, i'll kick off — we care about supporting very long docs, up to 128k tokens, for our legal+research pipelines. latency thresholds are tight for interactive UI, but batch processing is also important.
[00:30] Alex (Redwood AE): got it. priya and i will run through runtime behavior and tuning knobs. priya, want to cover the KV/cache and chunking overview?
[00:40] Priya (Redwood SE): sure, thanks. so, at 128k we typically treat the input as a sequence of chunks — roughly 4k-16k depending on model and attention strategy. key point: continuous KV cache lets us avoid recomputing past tokens, but memory and sharding become the limit.
[01:05] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): quick q — when you say sharding, are we talking across GPUs or across host processes? how does that impact cross-attention latency for an interactive query?
[01:20] Priya (Redwood SE): primarily across GPUs in Dedicated or on-prem setups. we shard KV by layer and by head groups; cross-GPU orchestration adds a small hop, typically a few ms, but can add jitter under heavy throughput. for interactive UI we recommend smaller chunk sizes and single-GPU hot path for the last N tokens to keep tail latency low.
[01:45] Samantha (Atlas CTO): hmm ok. our infra is k8s + private vpc, we need to know network egress and allowlist steps. priya verma will provide details after.
[01:55] Priya Verma (Atlas Infra): yep, we'll share firewall rules. also curious about quantization — can you run 4-bit for 128k without quality cliffs?
[02:10] Priya (Redwood SE): there are tradeoffs. quantization reduces memory so you can fit larger KV cache per GPU. 4-bit PTQ/LLM quant tends to introduce small perplexity drift; for retrieval-augmented generation it's often acceptable, but for safety-critical legal text you might prefer 8-bit or mixed: 8-bit for attention/query/projection matrices, 4-bit for feed-forward to maximize memory. we have recommended quant profiles per model that we can share.
[02:43] Daniel (Atlas Product): how about chunking strategies? do we keep overlapping windows, or a sliding attention approach?
[02:52] Priya (Redwood SE): overlapping windows (like 512–1024 overlap) give better context continuity but increase compute. alternative is hierarchical retrieval: index doc chunks and only load a focused window plus a condensed summary of earlier chunks. for 128k we often combine: a sparse retrieval for distal context + dense last-window with full KV.
[03:18] Alex (Redwood AE): i'll add that routing policies can route interactive requests to a lower-latency variant (smaller context model) and fallback to full long-run batch for heavy jobs. that buys you SLA guarantees.
[03:32] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): curious about batching — our workload is mixed interactive and nightly batch. how should we configure batching windows?
[03:40] Priya (Redwood SE): continuous batching helps. for interactive paths we use micro-batch (10–50ms) to keep latency sub-200ms; batch jobs can take larger windows and better kernel utilization. there's a sweet spot: higher batch sizes improve throughput but hurt p95/p99. we can tune autoscaling to add burst capacity for peak batching.
[04:02] Samantha (Atlas CTO): any real numbers you can share for 128k throughput/latency? ballpark is fine.
[04:10] Alex (Redwood AE): ballpark depends on model and quant. for a 128k run with a Llama-class 70B: - unquantized, single GPU, streaming last-window only: interactive p95 ~300–600ms for last-window responses but full document scans take minutes if you process everything serially. - with sharded KV across 4 GPUs and 8-bit quant, end-to-end for a full pass can be ~30–90s depending on prompt complexity. with specialized kernels and batching you can get better throughput. these are rough.
[04:47] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): 30–90s for full pass sounds reasonable for batch, but for our UI we need <500ms for followups. you mentioned hot-path single-GPU for last n tokens — how do we warm cache?
[05:00] Priya (Redwood SE): cache warm strategies: precompute first-pass embeddings and summary tokens, keep a rolling cache for active users, and prefetch predicted next-chunk KV into the hot GPU. also, partial KV snapshots can be stored in fast NVMe for quick reload. warm cache reduces lookups to memory copies instead of recompute.
[05:25] Daniel (Atlas Product): any special attention optimizations you use? linear attention approximations?
[05:30] Priya (Redwood SE): we use a mix. for exact attention we rely on optimized FlashAttention kernels; for very long context we employ chunked attention with rotary embeddings, block-sparse attention approximations, and memory-compressed attention for distal tokens. tradeoff: approximations save O(N^2) compute but can lose nuance for close-token dependencies.
[05:56] Samantha (Atlas CTO): how intrusive are those changes to model weights? do we need model retraining?
[06:03] Priya (Redwood SE): generally no retraining; these are runtime kernel and attention mask strategies. sometimes we do small finetunes to adapt to quantization but not required for most models.
[06:15] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): what about fallback and graceful degradation if Dedicated capacity is full?
[06:22] Alex (Redwood AE): our smart routing can fallback to hosted variants, or to smaller context models, or queue requests with priority. for latency-sensitive endpoints we prefer to reserve dedicated capacity. we can also route to a lower-cost model for non-critical queries.
[06:40] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): network constraints: for on-prem VPC we will need an offline benchmark mode. can you run without external control plane?
[06:50] Priya (Redwood SE): yes, Private mode supports an air-gapped deployment with a customer-managed control plane. we have a runbook for on-prem benchmarks where the harness runs inside your cluster and pushes metrics to a local prometheus or to Redwood temporarily over a secure pipe — we'll provide details.
[07:10] Samantha (Atlas CTO): great. can you outline the benchmark plan now?
[07:15] Alex (Redwood AE): plan: 1) Atlas shares representative doc samples and token distribution; 2) Redwood runs harness with three configs: (a) single-GPU last-window hot-path, (b) sharded KV 4-GPU 8-bit quant, (c) sharded KV 8-GPU mixed quant for highest throughput; 3) measure p50/p95/p99 latency for interactive queries, and end-to-end batch times; 4) produce a tuning doc with chunk sizes, overlap, and quant recommendations.
[07:45] Priya (Redwood SE): also we'll include memory profiles and KV cache eviction behavior. we'll log where jitter spikes — often due to cross-host collectives or NVLink saturation.
[07:58] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): NVLink is limited in our racks; do you support PCIe-only setups?
[08:05] Priya (Redwood SE): yes, we support PCIe-only; expect slightly higher cross-GPU latency. tuning: prefer fewer shards per layer and increase batch window so collectives amortize cost.
[08:20] Samantha (Atlas CTO): about security — where does data live during benchmarking? we need end-to-end encryption and KMS control.
[08:28] Alex (Redwood AE): we support customer-managed KMS, HSM integration, and encrypt data at rest. for Private we never store your raw prompts in Redwood-managed storage unless explicitly opted-in. we'll send SOC2 and ISO docs and a short PPT on key management.
[08:45] Daniel (Atlas Product): in terms of instrumentation, can we get token-level latency and cost breakdowns in the console?
[08:52] Priya (Redwood SE): yes, per-route and per-model dashboards show token-level breakdowns, KV miss rates, batching efficiency, and cost estimates. we'll share a sample dashboard screenshot.
[09:05] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): practical question — if we shard KV across many GPUs to hit memory for 128k, does that increase chance of OOM from transient spikes?
[09:15] Priya (Redwood SE): it can. mitigation: memory margin, dynamic eviction policies, and adaptive chunking. we also support spilling to SSD with fast reloads, though that increases latency. use-case dependent.
[09:30] Samantha (Atlas CTO): ok. walk me through an example: user uploads a 100k token doc and asks a question — what path does Redwood take end-to-end?
[09:40] Alex (Redwood AE): simplified: 1) ingestion: doc is chunked into X chunks and indexed; 2) retrieval: relevant chunks are selected; 3) runtime: relevant chunks streamed into model with KV cache; 4) last-window response done on hot GPU; 5) if model needs wider context it triggers background batch passes and updates output, or returns a partial answer. UX pattern: return preliminary answer fast, then update if broader scan changes answer.
[10:12] Daniel (Atlas Product): partial answers with updates are fine — we can signal confidence.
[10:18] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): any guidance on chunk size for legal docs? we have many dense passages where context matters across paragraph boundaries.
[10:26] Priya (Redwood SE): for dense legal text, we recommend larger chunk size (8k–16k) with 512–1024 overlap, plus semantic indexing to pull in related chunks. that balances coherence vs compute.
[10:42] Samantha (Atlas CTO): final question on QA/regression after quantization — how do you measure semantic drift?
[10:50] Priya (Redwood SE): we run eval suites: retrieval-augmented generation metrics, ROUGE/accurcy-like checks, and domain-specific checks (legal clause extraction). we also support human evals for high-sensitivity flows. we'll tie regressions to alerts in Redwood Optimize so you can roll back a quant config.
[11:12] Alex (Redwood AE): ok let's recap next steps — send benchmark harness, Atlas shares samples and networking details, Redwood runs three configs, and we'll reconvene with results. any final comments?
[11:28] Samantha (Atlas CTO): sounds good, thanks.
[11:32] Miguel (Atlas ML Eng): thanks, appreciate the detail.
[11:34] Priya (Redwood SE): we'll follow up with the quant matrix and chunking suggestions.
[11:38] Alex (Redwood AE): thanks everyone — meeting ended.
